newsitem.title: Croatia: Croatia opposition edge Tudjman party in Zagreb.
newsitem.headline: Croatia opposition edge Tudjman party in Zagreb.

text.p: An opposition coalition edged President Franjo Tudjman's nationalist party in key elections for the city assembly of the Croatian capital Zagreb, according to a final unofficial count announced on Monday.

The disclosure reversed the order of finish reported by the state electoral commission a few hours before in which it said the ruling HDZ had beaten the allied Social Democrats (SDP) and Social Liberals (HSLS) by a razor-thin margin.

State electoral commission chairman Ivan Mrkonjic announced that the SDP had finished with 24.18 percent and HSLS 12.58 percent in Sunday's election for a combined 36.76 percent while the HDZ tallied 35.67.

This did not necessarily mean the opposition would take over the powerful Zagreb regional government since the HDZ re-emerged as the biggest single vote-getter and its rivals fell well short of a viable majority.

With the result so close, any change of power looked fraught with problems in a country where effective one-party rule with a democratic veneer has prevailed for decades -- communists until 1990 and nationalists since then.

The SDP and HSLS led a seven-party bloc to victory over the HDZ in Zagreb's 1995 municipal elections. But Tudjman vetoed four opposition mayoral nominees on "national security" grounds and imposed provisional HDZ rule.

His manoeuvre brought accusations of authoritarianism and was condemned in the West. Tudjman argued the HDZ had won a "relative majority" while the opposition was an unstable mishmash of parties ranging from far left to far right.

Intense political manoeuvring loomed once again in Zagreb with each side seeking a broad enough bloc to rule Croatia's largest metropolis. It has a third of the population, almost half the industrial economy and a powerful patronage machine.

The HDZ, or Croatian Democratic Union, appeared to have lost two other big cities in the nationwide regional vote but only two of 21 county assemblies. HDZ-opposition stalemates surfaced in two counties hitherto run by the nationalists.

Former rebel Serbs took part in a Croatian election for the first time but voting in the enclave of Eastern Slavonia was delayed by technical glitches. The United Nations blamed the problem on the Zagreb government, which rejected the complaint.

Serbs in Eastern Slavonia, to be reintegrated in Croatia this summer after a period under U.N. protection, got an extra day to vote on Monday to compensate for organisational bungling that shut down balloting for hours on Sunday.

Pre-election polls hinted that the Social Democrats and Social Liberals, riding discontent over corruption and irregular privatisation, could upset the HDZ in Zagreb and a few other major cities in the republic of 4.7 million.

HDZ and opposition leaders had no immediate comment after Mrkonjic's announcement. The SDP and HSLS took issue with some results favouring the HDZ reported earlier on Monday, saying they suspected ballot-rigging.

Whether the SDP and HSLS eventually take power in Zagreb, as an opposition bloc did in Serbia's capital Belgrade after decades of Socialist rule, might depend on whether they can lure the moderate Peasant Party (HSS) to their cause.
The HSS polled 8.6 percent, but it has rejected alliances involving Social Democrats because of their communist past.

Although the Social Democrats made gains in several large cities, the overall election outcome reaffirmed that, despite serious social dislocations, most Croats are conservative and wedded to stability and strong leadership, the HDZ's fortes.

Tudjman, a former communist general, led Croatia in a successful 1991 war for independence from Serbian-led federal Yugoslavia. The HDZ relied heavily on his enduring charisma as "Father of the Nation" in the latest election campaign.

In Eastern Slavonia, the spokesman for the U.N. Transitional Authority in Eastern Slavonia said UNTAES was "very disappointed with the inadequate and incomplete support of the Croatian side in these election.
"...Packages of ballots were misdirected and voting lists were not corrected," spokesman Philip Arnold said.
A Croatian state election commission official rejected the U.N. complaint, insisting Zagreb had provided the number of ballot forms requested by UNTAES on the eve of the vote.

On Sunday, UNTAES suggested local Serb nationalist leaders were at fault. It chided them for failing to endorse the elections until the last minute, causing a belated spate of voter registration that fouled up planners.
